## Abstract

This study sought to determine whether the timing of spring green-up in Wapusk National Park (Manitoba, Canada) shifted between 2001 and 2024, and how strongly its year-to-year variation is associated with snowmelt timing and spring temperature.
Mid-green-up, defined as the day on which smoothed MODIS NDVI reaches half of its seasonal amplitude above a snow-free dormant baseline, was estimated for 300 land pixels stratified by land cover and aggregated to an area-weighted value for the drier part of the park in each year.
The analysis was pre-registered before any trend or driver relationship in the response was examined.
Mid-green-up averaged day of year (DOY) 180 (SD 7.5 days) and showed no detectable trend, with a Theil–Sen slope of +0.03 days/yr (95% CI −0.33 to +0.47); across 24 processing specifications the lower bound ranged from −0.33 to −0.72 days/yr, and a pre-registered power analysis put the minimum detectable trend near 0.9 days/yr, so the result rules out large shifts rather than demonstrating stability.
Later ERA5-Land snow-off was associated with later green-up (5.4 days per standard deviation, R² = 0.52), and April–May thawing degree days at Churchill accounted for a further 25% of the variance (BCa 95% CI 8–47%), for a combined R² of 0.77 and a leave-one-year-out error of 4.1 days; the size of the warmth association, however, depended on how the temperature window was drawn.
These associations held across all 24 specifications, under resampling of pixels, and with the two most influential years removed, and the series agreed with the MCD12Q2 product (r = 0.90), which is derived from the same sensor and therefore serves as a consistency check rather than independent validation.
A supplementary study ran a sandboxed coding agent for 33 iterations to improve the green-up extractor on synthetic data; its candidate generalised to held-out synthetic data but traded away interannual fidelity on real pixels, and the run yields concrete lessons for using agents in research pipelines.

## Introduction

Wapusk National Park lies on the western coast of Hudson Bay, in the transition between boreal forest and Arctic tundra, and its vegetation supports polar bears that forage on land during the ice-free season, as well as caribou and nesting geese whose breeding success depends on the timing of high-quality forage.
Doiron et al. [-@doiron2013] demonstrated on Bylot Island that the date on which NDVI reaches 50% of its annual maximum predicts the peak in plant nitrogen concentration, and Mallory et al. [-@mallory2020] reported that the start of green-up on the Qamanirjuaq caribou calving grounds, north-west of Hudson Bay, advanced by 7.25 days between 2004 and 2016, with migration and calving advancing alongside it.
Whether green-up has advanced in Wapusk, however, has not been established, and an earlier exploratory notebook in this repository fitted linear trends to a raw half-maximum NDVI date and produced slopes that changed between runs of identical code.

This report therefore replaces that exploration with a pre-registered analysis built around two questions.
First, it estimates the trend in mid-green-up between 2001 and 2024, together with the smallest trend the record could detect.
Next, it tests whether snow-off timing is associated with interannual variation in mid-green-up, and whether spring thawing degree days account for variation beyond snow-off.
The report then examines the sensitivity of each answer to processing choices, influential years, and predictor sources, compares the series with the MODIS Land Cover Dynamics product, and sets out the limitations of the design.
Lastly, a supplementary study reports what happened when a coding agent was given one narrow part of the pipeline to improve, and what that experiment suggests about the role of agents in research.

## Study Area

Wapusk National Park covers 11,475 km² of coastal lowland south and east of Churchill, Manitoba (57.1–58.8° N, 92.3–93.9° W).
The boundary used here is the Canada Lands Survey System administrative polygon published by Natural Resources Canada under the Open Government Licence (Canada).
Peatland and fen dominate the landscape, with shrub and graminoid tundra near the coast, lichen-dominated heath on raised beach ridges, and open spruce forest in the south and west.
Among randomly drawn 500 m pixels with little open water, ESA WorldCover classifies 57% as herbaceous wetland, 33% as shrub or grassland, 7% as moss and lichen, and 2% as tree cover (@fig-study-area).

![Wapusk National Park and the 300 sample pixels, coloured by land-cover stratum.](../results/figures/study_area.png){#fig-study-area width=55%}

## Data

All satellite and reanalysis inputs were accessed through Google Earth Engine [@gorelick2017].
Daily surface reflectance came from MOD09GA collection 6.1 [@vermote2021mod09ga], from which NDVI [@tucker1979] was computed from bands 1 and 2; MCD43A4 collection 6.1 nadir BRDF-adjusted reflectance [@schaaf2021mcd43a4] provided an alternative NDVI series.
MOD09GA coverage of the DOY 60–320 extraction window was incomplete in 2001 (244 of 261 days), 2002 (252), and 2022 (249).
Snow cover came from MOD10A1 collection 6.1 [@hall2021mod10a1] and from ERA5-Land daily aggregates [@munozsabater2021], which also supplied 2 m air temperature, snow depth, and precipitation.
The MCD12Q2 collection 6.1 Land Cover Dynamics product [@friedl2022mcd12q2] served only as a comparison.
Surface water came from the JRC Global Surface Water occurrence layer [@pekel2016], and land cover from ESA WorldCover 10 m v200 [@zanaga2022].
Daily mean temperature, precipitation, and snow on the ground at Churchill came from Environment and Climate Change Canada climate stations 5060600 (2001–2005) and 5060608 (2006–2024), with station 5060595 filling gaps.

## Methods

Every method below, its peer-reviewed basis, and the sensitivity test behind each parameter that the literature does not fix are documented in `docs/methods_justification.md`.
Analyses added after the confirmatory run are marked as post-hoc and listed in @sec-deviations.

### Pixel Sample and Target Population

Per-pixel phenology was estimated on a fixed sample rather than on a park-wide mean, because a mean over whichever pixels happen to be cloud-free on a given day mixes landscapes with different phenology from one day to the next.
Candidate pixel centres were drawn at random (seed 20261014) from the 53,164 MODIS 500 m grid cells inside the boundary, and the water fraction and modal WorldCover class of each candidate's exact footprint were computed at native resolution.
Pixels with more than 10% JRC surface water (occurrence above 50%) were excluded, which removed 28% of candidates (1,701 of 6,000), as were pixels outside the four strata, and the first 75 remaining candidates in each stratum (forest, shrub and grassland, wetland, moss and lichen) were retained.
The target population is therefore the drier land of the park, roughly 70% of its area, rather than the park as a whole, and the lake-rich and coastal-margin pixels excluded by the water screen may differ systematically from those retained.
Estimates were weighted by each stratum's share of dry land, following standard stratified estimation [@olofsson2014]; because ESA WorldCover maps herbaceous wetland with a user's accuracy of only 23–31% [@worldcoverpvr2022], the strata serve as a sampling design rather than as validated land-cover classes, which affects precision but not the validity of the weighted estimates.
The sample is committed as `data/aoi/sample_points.geojson`, so every run uses identical pixels.

### NDVI and Quality Masking

Two quality masks were applied to MOD09GA.
The strict (primary) mask retained a pixel only where the `state_1km` cloud state was clear or unset, no cloud shadow, internal cloud, MOD35 snow, internal snow, or cloud-adjacency flag was set, cirrus was absent or small, the sensor zenith angle was below 45°, and the `QC_500m` MODLAND flag indicated ideal or less-than-ideal quality.
Bit definitions follow the MOD09 Collection 6 user guide; the 45° view-angle screen addresses the documented dependence of daily MODIS NDVI on viewing geometry [@norris2020] and is stricter than the product's own 60° high-view flag.
The lenient mask kept only the cloud-state, internal cloud, internal snow, and MODLAND conditions.
The snow flags were also retained as a separate band, so that snow-covered days could anchor the dormant baseline rather than simply disappear.
Under the strict mask, 12% of pixel-days between DOY 60 and 320 were usable, compared with 18% under the lenient mask.

### Green-Up Extraction

For each pixel, a dormant baseline was defined as the 5th percentile of all snow-free NDVI observations outside DOY 150–250, pooled across years; the concept of a pixel-specific winter NDVI that replaces lower values follows Beck et al. [-@beck2006], while the percentile rule follows the dormant-value step of MCD12Q2 [@gray2019guide].
Within the DOY 91–300 window of each pixel-year, observed NDVI below the baseline was raised to it, and snow-flagged days before the first and after the last snow-free observation were entered as baseline values.
The primary smoother interpolated these points to a daily series and applied a Savitzky–Golay filter (31-day window, second-order polynomial) with two upper-envelope passes, in which observations falling below the fitted curve were treated as residual cloud contamination [@chen2004; @jonsson2004].
Chen et al. [-@chen2004] recommended a window of about 90 days for 10-day composites; the shorter window was chosen because daily data resolve the rapid, melt-driven rise that a 90-day window would flatten, and windows from 15 to 91 days were tested.
Mid-green-up was the first day before the seasonal peak on which the curve reached the baseline plus 50% of the amplitude [@white1997], interpolated linearly between days.
Pixel-years with fewer than 15 snow-free observations, an amplitude below 0.10 NDVI (the MCD12Q2 floor), or a crossing at the window start were treated as missing.
@fig-example-fits shows three randomly drawn pixel-years.

This definition departs from Doiron et al. [-@doiron2013], whose abstract defines the metric as the date at which 1 km AVHRR NDVI "reached 50% of their annual maximum".
In Wapusk that crossing cannot be defined once snow is masked, because the snow-free dormant NDVI (median 0.42) exceeds half the summer peak (median 0.60) in 92% of pixels; with snow left in, it would mark snowmelt rather than growth.
The amplitude form avoids this, does not depend on the NDVI of snow, and is analogous to the MCD12Q2 `MidGreenup` metric, which applies the same 50% rule to EVI2 [@gray2019guide; @moon2019].

![Three randomly drawn pixel-years under the primary specification, showing snow-free observations, snow anchors at the baseline, the Savitzky–Golay fit, and the estimated mid-green-up.](../results/figures/example_fits.png){#fig-example-fits}

The annual value was the weighted median across valid pixels, a plug-in estimator in which each pixel's weight was its stratum's share of dry land divided by the number of valid pixels in that stratum that year, which corrects for the equal allocation of the sample across strata.
A year with fewer than 30% valid pixels would have been treated as missing; none was, as between 227 and 300 of the 300 pixels contributed in each year.

### Predictors

The pre-registered snow-off date was the day after the last day between DOY 60 and 212 on which park-mean ERA5-Land snow cover was at or above 50%.
ERA5-Land was chosen over the Churchill station before any relationship with green-up was examined, for three reasons: the station lacked a usable spring snow-on-ground record in 9 of 24 years; where present, station snow-off correlated with ERA5-Land snow-off at only r = 0.58 (and with MODIS snow-off at r = 0.56); and ERA5-Land and MODIS snow-off (the day after the last day park-mean MOD10A1 NDSI was at or above 0.4, the conventional snow threshold of @hall2002) agreed at r = 0.81 despite their independent sources.
ERA5-Land derives snow cover from modelled snow depth and is known to overestimate snow-cover duration [@urraca2023] and spring snow mass [@kouki2023] in the Northern Hemisphere; its snow-off averaged 3.3 days later than MODIS snow-off here, so it is used as an index of interannual variation rather than as an absolute melt date.
Neither primary predictor relies on the MODIS snow flags that shape the NDVI series, which limits, although it does not remove, any mechanical coupling between snow-off and green-up, since the snow anchors still place each pixel's dormant period before its own MODIS-detected melt.
Thawing degree days (TDD) were the sum of positive daily mean temperatures at Churchill over DOY 91–151 (1 April–31 May in common years, one day earlier in leap years), a window chosen to end before the earliest plausible mid-green-up, following evidence that snowmelt and spring temperature jointly shape tundra spring phenology [@assmann2019; @bjorkman2015]; 14 of 1,464 station-days were filled from ERA5-Land through a daily linear calibration.
In four years (2002, 2004, 2009, and 2012) ERA5-Land snow-off fell after DOY 151, so in those years the TDD window measures warmth before melt.
The spliced station series matches the homogenized AHCCD Churchill record [@vincent2020] closely (April–May mean temperature r = 0.9995, mean difference −0.17 °C, 2001–2020).

### Statistical Analysis

The trend in mid-green-up (H1) was estimated as a Theil–Sen slope [@sen1968] with a 95% confidence interval, accompanied by Mann–Kendall tests with trend-free pre-whitening [@yue2002], as pre-registered; because trend-free pre-whitening can inflate Type I error under strong autocorrelation [@burger2017], the uncorrected test, the Hamed–Rao variance correction [@hamed1998], and pre-whitening [@yuewang2002] were added post hoc.
Because a trend estimate from 24 years is only informative relative to the smallest trend the series could reveal, the minimum detectable trend was simulated before the response was examined, using the detrended interannual standard deviation of the MCD12Q2 series (9.2 days) and an AR(1) noise model [@weatherhead1998]; Mann–Kendall reached 80% power at α = 0.05 only for trends of 0.9 days/yr or larger.
Post hoc, the conventional version based on the series' own detrended variability (SD 7.6 days) gave a minimum detectable trend of 0.70–0.75 days/yr for lag-1 autocorrelations between 0 and 0.3.

The association with snow-off (H2) was tested with ordinary least squares on standardized predictors, and the added contribution of TDD (H3) with a nested F-test, which is the primary basis for inference on H3, and a percentile bootstrap confidence interval (5,000 resamples of years) for the change in R² [@efron1993]; because a percentile interval for a quantity bounded at zero is biased in small samples, a BCa interval was added post hoc.
Because warmer springs also melt snow earlier, the explained variance was partitioned into unique and shared components by commonality analysis [@seibold1979; @raymukherjee2014], which, as pre-registered, is read as a single causal chain from warmth through melt to green-up rather than as evidence of independent effects.
Both models were evaluated by leave-one-year-out cross-validation against a long-term mean.

### Robustness Grid, Comparison Product, and Post-Hoc Checks

H1 to H3 were re-estimated across 24 specifications formed by three smoothers (Savitzky–Golay; a double logistic with fixed baseline after @beck2006 and @zhang2003; a weighted Whittaker smoother after @eilers2003 and @atzberger2011), two thresholds (50% and 15% of amplitude), two masks (strict and lenient), and two aggregations (weighted median and weighted mean).
Alternative predictor sources (station snow-off gap-filled from ERA5-Land, and ERA5-Land TDD), an NBAR-based NDVI series, and per-stratum trends were pre-registered sensitivity checks.
Agreement with MCD12Q2 `MidGreenup_1`, restricted to best- and good-quality retrievals, was computed between the two park-wide annual series and, at the pixel-year scale, over matched pixel-years; because MCD12Q2 is derived from the same MODIS reflectance (as NBAR EVI2), agreement with it demonstrates consistency between retrievals rather than accuracy.

Two sets of checks were added after the confirmatory run (@sec-deviations).
A methods audit added one-at-a-time tests of every parameter the literature does not fix (smoothing window, Whittaker λ, baseline percentile and pooling, view-angle screen, minimum observations and amplitude, water screen, stratum weighting, snow-cover threshold, TDD window, and exclusion of the 2022–2024 Terra drift years).
A referee report then prompted the following:

* a bootstrap over pixels within strata within years, carrying retrieval variability through H1–H3;
* bootstrap intervals for the commonality components and the combined-model coefficients;
* influence diagnostics and the removal of the most influential years, together with rank and logarithmic transforms of TDD;
* the 15 years with genuine station snow-off, and MODIS snow-off as a predictor;
* separate models for the wetland and non-wetland strata, and the frequency with which snow anchors constrain the crossing;
* the trend over 2004–2016 for comparison with Mallory et al. [-@mallory2020].

## Results

### Agreement with MCD12Q2

The park-wide series agreed closely with the park-wide MCD12Q2 series (r = 0.90), although it ran on average 8.3 days later (SD 4.0 days); at the pixel-year scale, agreement was weaker (r = 0.55, MAE 10.1 days, bias +8.6 days, n = 5,126).
The annual offset showed no trend (−0.03 days/yr, CI −0.26 to +0.31), and averaged 9.2 days in the Terra drift years of 2022–2024, within the range of earlier years, so a time-varying offset does not appear to affect the trend or driver analyses.
The NBAR series gave similar agreement (matched annual r = 0.91, pixel-year r = 0.63).
The offset is consistent with the strict mask, which discards early-season observations near cloud and snow, and with MCD12Q2's use of EVI2 with its own baseline.

![Pixel-year agreement between this study and MCD12Q2 MidGreenup. The dashed line marks one-to-one agreement.](../results/figures/validation_scatter.png){#fig-validation width=55%}

### Trend (H1)

Mid-green-up ranged from DOY 165 in 2006 to DOY 196 in 2009 (mean 180, SD 7.5 days) and showed no trend: the Theil–Sen slope was +0.03 days/yr (95% CI −0.33 to +0.47), or a total shift of +0.8 days over the record (CI −7.5 to +10.9 days), with Mann–Kendall p between 0.60 and 0.86 under all four variants (@fig-series).
The primary interval excludes advances faster than about a third of a day per year, and it is narrower than the pre-registered power analysis anticipated because the detrended variability of the primary series is lower than that of MCD12Q2 (7.6 against 9.2 days).
That precision is, however, specific to the primary specification: across the 24 specifications the lower bound ranged from −0.33 to −0.72 days/yr, and in 14 of them it reached below −0.56 days/yr.
Following the pre-registered interpretation rule, the result is reported as no trend detectable at this sensitivity rather than as evidence that green-up has not changed.
The MCD12Q2 series (+0.10 days/yr, CI −0.40 to +0.67), the NBAR series (−0.04 days/yr, CI −0.40 to +0.43), and each land-cover stratum, whose slopes ranged from +0.01 (wetland) to +0.17 days/yr (forest), all had intervals spanning zero.

![Park-wide mid-green-up from this study and from MCD12Q2, with the Theil–Sen trend of the primary series.](../results/figures/greenup_series.png){#fig-series}

### Snow-Off and Spring Warmth (H2 and H3)

Snow-off was associated with roughly half of the interannual variation in mid-green-up (@fig-drivers): each standard deviation (15 days) of later snow-off corresponded to 5.4 days later green-up (95% CI 3.1–7.7, p < 0.001, R² = 0.52, adjusted R² = 0.49), or about 0.35 days per day of snow-off.
Adding TDD increased R² by 0.25 (F = 22.3, p < 0.001; percentile bootstrap CI 0.09–0.48, BCa CI 0.08–0.47), and in the combined model each standard deviation (48 degree-days) of additional April–May warmth was associated with green-up 4.1 days earlier (bootstrap CI 2.4–5.5), while snow-off retained a coefficient of 3.6 days per standard deviation (CI 1.4–5.7).
The two-predictor model explained 77% of the variance (adjusted R² = 0.74), and its leave-one-year-out error of 4.1 days compares with 5.7 days for snow-off alone and 7.6 days for the long-term mean.
Of the explained variance, commonality analysis attributed 24% uniquely to snow-off (bootstrap CI 6–46%), 33% uniquely to TDD (11–65%), and 43% to their shared component (12–69%); in units of total variance these are 0.19, 0.25, and 0.33.
The lag between snow-off and mid-green-up showed no trend (+0.42 days/yr, CI −0.30 to +1.02), although that interval is too wide to be informative.

![Mid-green-up against ERA5-Land snow-off and Churchill April–May thawing degree days, with simple least-squares lines.](../results/figures/drivers_scatter.png){#fig-drivers}

### Robustness

None of the 24 specifications produced a trend whose confidence interval excluded zero, with slopes ranging from −0.05 to +0.11 days/yr (@fig-multiverse), whereas H2 and H3 were supported in all 24, with snow-off effects between 5.4 and 8.2 days per standard deviation and TDD increments in R² between 0.12 and 0.32.
The 15% threshold and the lenient mask produced larger snow-off slopes, but under the strict mask R² barely changed (0.515 to 0.523 for the Savitzky–Golay median), so the larger slopes mainly reflect greater variance in the 15% dates rather than tighter coupling to melt.
Substituting station snow-off or ERA5-Land TDD left all three conclusions unchanged (combined R² of 0.67 and 0.79, respectively).
In the post-hoc parameter tests, every trend interval spanned zero, including the variant that excluded the Terra drift years (+0.21 days/yr, CI −0.29 to +0.79), and snow-off remained significant throughout; two variants lost years, as the 30° view-angle screen left 21 valid years and the 25-observation minimum left 19.

The referee-prompted checks qualified, but did not overturn, the driver results.

* **Retrieval variability:** resampling pixels within strata within years produced narrow intervals (H1 slope −0.04 to +0.09 days/yr; snow-off 5.2–5.6 days per SD; ΔR² 0.23–0.27), so uncertainty in the annual values is small relative to the sampling of years.
* **Influence:** 2006 had the largest Cook's distance (0.30), followed by 2012, 2004, and 2009; removing 2004 and 2009 together, the two latest years with near-zero TDD, reduced the snow-off R² to 0.36 (p = 0.003) and left the TDD increment at 0.32.
  Rank- and log-transformed TDD gave increments of 0.27 and 0.25.
* **Predictor sources:** with only the 15 years of genuine station snow-off, the snow-off association weakened to 3.6 days per SD (R² = 0.27, p = 0.05) while the TDD increment remained (0.38, p = 0.004); MODIS snow-off as the predictor gave 5.5 days per SD (R² = 0.54).
* **Wetland surfaces:** if standing meltwater in fens delayed the NDVI rise, the association would be stronger in wetland pixels, yet the snow-off effect was similar in the wetland stratum alone (5.5 days per SD) and in the remaining strata (5.2 days per SD).
  Snow anchors did not fix the dates mechanically, as the median crossing fell 24 days after a pixel's first clear observation and only 2.3% fell within a week of it.
* **Temperature window:** the contribution of spring warmth was the most sensitive result; ending the TDD window on DOY 135 (15 May) rather than DOY 151 reduced the increment in R² to 0.09 (p = 0.04), and replacing TDD with homogenized April–May mean temperature gave 0.12 (p = 0.04, n = 18).
  A window ending on DOY 166 gave 0.34 but overlaps green-up in the earliest years, so it is partly circular and is not interpreted.

In the exploratory analysis, maximum spring snow depth (Spearman ρ = 0.08, n = 24) and spring precipitation (ρ = −0.19, n = 22, missing 2007 and 2009) showed no association with green-up.

![Theil–Sen slope and 95% CI for H1 across all 24 specifications. The pre-registered primary specification is shown in orange.](../results/figures/multiverse.png){#fig-multiverse}

## Discussion

Overall, the results suggest that green-up timing in the drier part of Wapusk varies far more from one spring to the next than it has changed across the 24-year record.
A spring with late snowmelt and little April–May warmth, such as 2009, delayed mid-green-up by about two weeks relative to the mean, whereas the early melt and warm spring of 2006 advanced it by a similar margin; the year-to-year standard deviation of 7.5 days is comparable to the total change of −7.5 to +10.9 days that the primary interval allows over the whole record.

The comparison with Mallory et al. [-@mallory2020] is closer than the full-record interval implies.
Over their 2004–2016 window, the primary mid-green-up series trended at −0.31 days/yr (CI −1.57 to +0.83), and onset at the 15% threshold trended at −0.27 to −0.61 days/yr across smoothers and masks, both compatible with their 0.56 days/yr advance in the start of green-up, although the short window leaves every estimate very uncertain.
Taken together, these results suggest that the decade they studied may have been one of earlier springs in this region, and that over the longer record the advance did not persist in Wapusk; this pattern resembles the long-term record from Zackenberg in north-east Greenland, where earlier advances in spring phenology have given way to little directional change [@schmidt2023].
Assmann et al. [-@assmann2019] found that phenology advanced only at sites where snowmelt advanced, and that regional sea ice did not explain the variation, so the absence of a trend in Wapusk is more plausibly connected to the absence of a trend in local snowmelt than to Hudson Bay ice, although this study did not test either directly.

The commonality analysis is consistent with the pre-registered reading of a single chain from spring warmth through snowmelt to green-up: 43% of the explained variance is shared between the two predictors, and neither unique component is precisely estimated.
This study cannot separate the effect of warmth before melt from its effect on the pace of growth after melt, because in four years the temperature window closed before snow-off, and because the warmth association depended strongly on where the window ended.
For the caribou and geese that rely on early-season forage, the results suggest that the timing of high-quality forage in a given year is reasonably predictable from spring conditions, with a cross-validated error of about four days, and that in 20 of the 24 years both predictors were available by the end of May.

## Limitations

There are seven main limitations to this research.
First, 24 years of data offer limited sensitivity to trends: the pre-registered power analysis put the minimum detectable trend at about 0.9 days/yr, the conventional version at 0.70–0.75 days/yr, and most specifications in the robustness grid cannot exclude advances of 0.56 days/yr.
Second, the analysis is not blind, as the earlier notebook fitted trends to a related metric and the pooled distribution of green-up dates under each specification was viewed before pre-registration, although no annual series, trend, or predictor relationship was examined.
Next, the driver models rest on 24 points, a few of which carry substantial influence; the snow-off association weakens when the two latest years are removed or when only genuine station data are used, and predictor error, which biases slopes toward zero, was assessed only by substituting alternative sources.
Furthermore, the predictors are coarse, as ERA5-Land resolves the park at roughly 9–11 km and overestimates snow duration, while the thawing degree days come from a single coastal station north of the park, and the warmth association depends on the choice of window.
In addition, the inference applies to the drier ~70% of the park, and the strata used to weight it are poorly mapped in wetland, which is the dominant class.
The absolute dates also depend on processing choices, with the strict and lenient masks differing by about nine days in the median, and agreement with MCD12Q2 demonstrates consistency between two MODIS retrievals rather than accuracy, since no ground phenology was available.
Lastly, the Terra platform has been drifting to earlier overpass times since it left its constellation in 2022, and while the NBAR series, the stable offset from MCD12Q2, and the trend excluding those years do not indicate a problem, the final years warrant caution.

## Conclusion

This study sought to establish whether green-up in Wapusk National Park has shifted since 2001 and how its year-to-year timing relates to snowmelt and spring warmth.
No trend was detectable across the 2001–2024 record under any of 24 processing specifications, although the record cannot exclude moderate advances of the size reported nearby for 2004–2016.
Snow-off timing and spring warmth together accounted for 77% of the interannual variation, consistent with a chain in which warm springs bring earlier melt and earlier green-up, although the contribution of warmth beyond snow-off was sensitive to how it was measured.
Future work could extend the record with Landsat and Sentinel-2 to increase sensitivity, add ground phenology from the Churchill area to move beyond consistency checks, and test whether these spring conditions predict the timing of caribou and goose use of the park.

## Deviations, Timeline, and Use of AI {#sec-deviations}

The pre-registration (`prereg.md`) was committed at 23:12:06 UTC on 14 October 2026 (commit `cba988e`), after the Earth Engine extraction finished at 23:08:41 UTC and per-pixel green-up dates, predictors, and the MCD12Q2-based power analysis had been computed, and four seconds before the confirmatory run began at 23:12:10 UTC.
The commit history makes this order verifiable, but the safeguard rests on that order rather than on elapsed time, because all of these steps were performed within a single working session.
The following analyses were added after the confirmatory run and are reported alongside it without replacing it: the one-at-a-time parameter tests and statistical robustness checks from a methods audit; the additional Mann–Kendall variants, the BCa interval, and the conventional minimum detectable trend; the AHCCD comparison; and the referee-prompted checks listed in the Methods.
The pre-registration's attribution of the percentile baseline was also corrected (to MCD12Q2, with Beck et al. for the concept), with no change to the method.
The analysis code, pre-registration, and first draft of this report were produced by an AI coding agent (Claude Code) working under the author's direction, and an AI referee reviewed the draft (`results/review.md`); the author is responsible for the research questions, design decisions, and conclusions.

## Supplementary Study: A Sandboxed Agent Loop for Method Development {.unnumbered}

This supplementary study asks what happens when a coding agent is given one narrow, well-defined part of a research pipeline to improve, and what can be learned from the result about using agents in research.
The task was the green-up extractor: turning gappy, noisy daily NDVI into a crossing date.
The study was kept entirely separate from the confirmatory analysis, and a fuller account, with recommendations, is in `autoresearch/LESSONS.md`.

### Design {.unnumbered}

The design follows the pattern of a single editable program judged by a fixed external evaluator, as in Karpathy's autoresearch [@karpathy2026] and AlphaEvolve [@novikov2025], with the held-out grading and rule-breaking checks emphasised by MLE-bench [@chan2024], rather than an agent-driven notebook.
In each iteration, a Claude Code agent could read the repository and edit only `src/wapusk_greenup/method.py`; it could not execute code, write other files, use the web, or read the held-out benchmark.
A driver outside the agent reverted any other change, verified the hashes of the evaluator and benchmark against a lock stored outside the repository, scored the candidate, and kept it only if the score fell.
The visible benchmark contained 1,800 synthetic pixel-seasons from three curve families, with cloud gaps resampled from 7,088 real strict-mask pixel-years, snow before melt, late snowfall, Gaussian noise, and negative outliers.
The score was the mean error against the known crossing, capped at 30 days, plus small penalties for line count and runtime.
After the loop, the candidate was frozen (SHA-256 `0d0d9af3…`) and scored once on held-out seeds and a fourth family built from normalised real NDVI seasons, then compared with the baseline on real pixels against four criteria fixed in advance in the pre-registration, although the operational definition of the melt-plausibility criterion was not, and was corrected once after its first run because it ended the snow season at the first cloudy day.

### Results {.unnumbered}

The loop ran for 33 iterations (3 in a smoke test and 30 in the main run) at an estimated usage of USD 17.90 at API list prices, about USD 0.54 per iteration; no iteration attempted an edit outside the permitted file.
Eight changes were kept, 20 were reverted because they did not lower the score, and in the last five iterations the agent reported that it had no further idea worth testing and made no edit (@fig-agent).
Three kept changes altered the method: the candidate ignores snow flags between melt and the first clear observation, on the reasoning that a brief snowfall hides vegetation without making it dormant (iteration 8); it lowers the amplitude floor from 0.10 to 0.05 NDVI, which mainly converts seasons that scored the 30-day failure penalty into estimates (iteration 9); and it takes the seasonal amplitude from a fit that discards strongly negative outliers, correcting the upward bias that the upper envelope introduces at the peak (iteration 16).
Four further kept changes (iterations 19, 26, 27, and 28) only removed or merged lines, leaving every estimate identical, and the agent described them openly as cleanups that would lower the score by 0.001 through the line-count penalty.

On synthetic data the candidate generalised modestly, as its error fell from 3.18 to 2.96 days on the visible benchmark and from 4.66 to 4.39 days on the held-out benchmark, where it outperformed all three baseline smoothers.
On the held-out family built from real season shapes, however, every method erred by 8.4–10.9 days against 2–4 days on the synthetic families, and the candidate's gain there was only 0.15 days, which suggests that the synthetic generators represented real seasons poorly.
On real pixels, the candidate improved pixel-year agreement with MCD12Q2 (MAE 9.7 against 10.1 days) but lowered the park-wide annual correlation (0.881 against 0.900) and placed 0.15% of pixel-years before the pixel's own snowmelt, so under the pre-registered rule it did not join the robustness grid.
A post-hoc ablation (@tbl-ablation) located the trade-off: iteration 8 improved held-out error and slightly raised annual agreement, whereas iteration 16 bought a lower pixel bias at the cost of interannual fidelity, and removing single changes from the frozen candidate showed that the components interact.
None of the versions moved the scientific conclusions, with H1 slopes of 0.005–0.042 days/yr, snow-off effects of 5.4–5.7 days per standard deviation, and TDD increments of 0.24–0.26.

| Version | Held-out error (days) | Annual r with MCD12Q2 | Pixel MAE (days) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Start (pre-registered Savitzky–Golay) | 4.66 | 0.900 | 10.11 |
| Iteration 8: ignore post-melt snow flags | 4.48 | 0.903 | 10.14 |
| Iteration 9: amplitude floor 0.05 | 4.45 | 0.902 | 10.28 |
| Iteration 16: robust amplitude rescaling | 4.40 | 0.881 | 9.63 |
| Frozen candidate (iteration 28) | 4.39 | 0.881 | 9.68 |

: Ablation of kept versions of the agent's extractor. Source: `results/tables/autoresearch_ablation.csv`. {#tbl-ablation}

![Left: visible score by iteration, with kept, reverted, and no-edit iterations. Right: held-out synthetic error against park-wide annual agreement with MCD12Q2 for each kept version (blue) and for the frozen candidate with one change removed (green).](../results/figures/autoresearch_dynamics.png){#fig-agent}

### What the Experiment Suggests {.unnumbered}

The experiment suggests five lessons for using agents in research pipelines, which `autoresearch/LESSONS.md` develops with recommendations.
First, enforcement belongs outside the agent and should be tested before the agent runs: the agent never tested the sandbox, so its clean record says little, whereas scripted adversarial agents demonstrated that the driver reverted forbidden edits, and the only enforcement failure in the project was a parsing bug in the driver itself, caught by the smoke test.
Second, a single scalar objective was gamed even by an agent that behaved transparently, through the line-count penalty and the fixed failure penalty, which argues for behavioural-equivalence checks and objectives whose cheapest improvement is the behaviour that is wanted.
Next, the proxy diverged from the science, since per-season accuracy improved while the interannual fidelity that the trend and driver analyses depend on declined, and a keep-if-lower rule discarded the version (iteration 8) that served the science best; scoring the downstream statistic directly and keeping a Pareto archive across objectives would address both.
Furthermore, benchmark realism, rather than search, was the binding constraint, as shown by the gap between synthetic and real-shaped seasons.
Lastly, keeping the agent off the inference path meant that none of its choices could influence the reported result, so the stability of the conclusions across its versions is a finding rather than a defence; this suggests that agents are most safely deployed on measurement and engineering problems with external ground truth, and kept away from steps where optimising a number is indistinguishable from searching for significance.
